{{Short description|Mathematics concept}}
{{Group theory sidebar |Discrete}}
[[Image:F2 Cayley Graph.svg|right|thumb|class=skin-invert-image|Diagram showing the [[Cayley graph]] for the free group on two generators.  Each vertex represents an element of the free group, and each edge represents multiplication by ''a'' or ''b''.]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''free group''' <math>F_S</math> over a given set <math>S</math> consists of all [[Word (group theory)|words]] that can be built from members of <math>S</math>, considering two words to be different unless their equality follows from the [[Group (mathematics)#Definition|group axioms]] (e.g. <math>st=suu^{-1}t</math> but <math>s\neq t^{-1}</math> for <math>s,t,u\in S</math>). The members of <math>S</math> are called '''generators''' of <math>F_S</math>, and the number of generators is the '''rank''' of the free group.
An arbitrary [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> is called '''free''' if it is [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to <math>F_S</math> for some [[subset]] <math>S</math> of <math>G</math>, that is, if there is a subset <math>S</math> of <math>G</math> such that every element of <math>G</math> can be written in exactly one way as a product of finitely many elements of <math>S</math> and their inverses (disregarding trivial variations such as <math>st=suu^{-1}t</math>).

A related but different notion is a [[free abelian group]]; both notions are particular instances of a [[free object]] from [[universal algebra]]. As such, free groups are defined by their [[Free group#Universal property|universal property]].

== History ==
Free groups first arose in the study of [[hyperbolic geometry]], as examples of [[Fuchsian group]]s (discrete groups acting by [[isometry|isometries]] on the [[Hyperbolic geometry|hyperbolic plane]]).  In an 1882 paper, [[Walther von Dyck]] pointed out that these groups have the simplest possible [[group presentation|presentations]].<ref>{{cite journal | last = von Dyck | first = Walther | author-link = Walther von Dyck | title = Gruppentheoretische Studien (Group-theoretical Studies) | journal = [[Mathematische Annalen]] | volume = 20 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–44 | year = 1882 | url = http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/index.php?id=11&PPN=GDZPPN002246724&L=1 | doi = 10.1007/BF01443322 | s2cid = 179178038 | access-date = 2015-09-01 | archive-date = 2016-03-04 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160304201754/http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/index.php?id=11&PPN=GDZPPN002246724&L=1 | url-status = dead }}</ref> The algebraic study of free groups was initiated by [[Jakob Nielsen (mathematician)|Jakob Nielsen]] in 1924, who gave them their name and established many of their basic properties.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Nielsen|first=Jakob|author-link=Jakob Nielsen (mathematician)|year=1917|title=Die Isomorphismen der allgemeinen unendlichen Gruppe mit zwei Erzeugenden|url=http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/index.php?id=11&PPN=GDZPPN002266873&L=1|journal=[[Mathematische Annalen]]|volume=78|issue=1|pages=385–397|doi=10.1007/BF01457113|jfm=46.0175.01|mr=1511907|s2cid=119726936|access-date=2015-09-01|archive-date=2016-03-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305141749/http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/index.php?id=11&PPN=GDZPPN002266873&L=1|url-status=dead}}

== Examples ==
The group <math>(\mathbb{Z},+)</math> of [[integer]]s is free of rank 1; a generating set is <math>S=\{1\}</math>. The integers are also a [[free abelian group]], although all free groups of rank <math>\geq 2</math> are non-abelian. A free group on a two-element set <math>S</math> occurs in the proof of the [[Banach–Tarski paradox]] and is described there.

On the other hand, any nontrivial finite group cannot be free, since the elements of a free generating set of a free group have infinite order.

In [[algebraic topology]], the [[fundamental group]] of a [[bouquet of circles|bouquet of ''k'' circles]] (a set of ''k'' loops having only one point in common) is the free group on a set of ''k'' elements.

== Construction ==
The '''free group''' <math>F_S</math> with '''free generating set''' <math>S</math> can be constructed as follows.  <math>S</math> is a set of symbols, and we suppose for every <math>s</math> in <math>S</math> there is a corresponding "inverse" symbol, <math>s^{-1}</math>, in a set <math>S^{-1}</math>. Let <math>T=S\cup S^{-1}</math>, and define a '''[[word (group theory)|word]]''' in <math>S</math> to be any written product of elements of <math>T</math>. That is, a word in <math>S</math> is an element of the [[monoid]] generated by <math>T</math>. The empty word is the word with no symbols at all. For example, if <math>S=\{a,b,c\}</math>, then <math>T=\{a,a^{-1},b,b^{-1},c,c^{-1}\}</math>, and
<math display=block>a b^3 c^{-1} c a^{-1} c\,</math>
is a word in <math>F_S</math>.

If an element of <math>S</math> lies immediately next to its inverse, the word may be simplified by omitting the <math>c,c^{-1}</math> pair:
<math display=block>a b^3 c^{-1} c a^{-1} c\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;a b^3 \, a^{-1} c.</math>
A word that cannot be simplified further is called '''reduced'''.

The free group <math>F_S</math> is defined to be the group of all reduced words in <math>S</math>, with [[concatenation]] of words (followed by reduction if necessary) as group operation.  The identity is the empty word.

A reduced word is called '''cyclically reduced''' if its first and last letter are not inverse to each other. Every word is [[Conjugacy class|conjugate]] to a cyclically reduced word, and a cyclically reduced conjugate of a cyclically reduced word is a cyclic permutation of the letters in the word.  For instance <math>b^{-1}abcb</math> is not cyclically reduced, but is conjugate to <math>abc</math>, which is cyclically reduced.  The only cyclically reduced conjugates of <math>abc</math> are <math>abc</math>, <math>bca</math>, and <math>cab</math>.

== Universal property ==
The free group <math>F_S</math> is the [[Universal (mathematics)|universal]] group generated by the set <math>S</math>.  This can be formalized by the following [[universal property]]: given any function <math>f</math> from <math>S</math> to a group <math>G</math>, there exists a unique [[group homomorphism|homomorphism]] <math>\varphi:F_S\to G</math> making the following [[commutative diagram|diagram]] commute (where the unnamed mapping denotes the [[Inclusion map|inclusion]] from <math>S</math> into <math>F_S</math>):
[[Image:Free Group Universal.svg|center|class=skin-invert-image|100px]]
That is, homomorphisms <math>F_S\to G</math> are in one-to-one correspondence with functions <math>S\to G</math>. For a non-free group, the presence of [[group presentation|relations]] would restrict the possible images of the generators under a homomorphism.

To see how this relates to the constructive definition, think of the mapping from <math>S</math> to <math>F_S</math> as sending each symbol to a word consisting of that symbol. To construct <math>\varphi</math> for the given <math>f</math>, first note that <math>\varphi</math> sends the empty word to the identity of <math>G</math> and it has to agree with <math>f</math> on the elements of <math>S</math>. For the remaining words (consisting of more than one symbol), <math>\varphi</math> can be uniquely extended, since it is a homomorphism, i.e., <math>\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)</math>.

The above property characterizes free groups up to [[isomorphism]], and is sometimes used as an alternative definition.  It is known as the [[universal property]] of free groups, and the generating set <math>S</math> is called a '''basis''' for <math>F_S</math>.  The basis for a free group is not uniquely determined.

Being characterized by a universal property is the standard feature of [[free object]]s in [[universal algebra]].  In the language of [[category theory]], the construction of the free group (similar to most constructions of free objects) is a [[functor]] from the [[category of sets]] to the [[category of groups]].  This functor is [[left adjoint]] to the [[forgetful functor]] from groups to sets.

==Facts and theorems==
Some properties of free groups follow readily from the definition:

#Any group <math>G</math> is the homomorphic image of some free group <math>F_S</math>. Let <math>S</math> be a set of ''[[Generating set of a group|generators]]'' of <math>G</math>. The natural map <math>\varphi</math>: <math>F_S\to G</math> is an [[epimorphism]], which proves the claim. Equivalently, <math>G</math> is isomorphic to a [[quotient group]] of some free group <math>F_S</math>. If <math>S</math> can be chosen to be finite here, then <math>G</math> is called [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]]. The kernel <math>\ker\varphi</math> is the set of all ''relations'' in the [[Presentation of a group|presentation]] of <math>G</math>; if <math>\ker\varphi</math> can be generated by the conjugates of finitely many elements of <math>F</math>, then <math>G</math> is finitely presented.
#If <math>S</math> has more than one element, then <math>F_S</math> is not [[abelian group|abelian]], and in fact the [[center of a group|center]] of <math>F_S</math> is trivial (that is, consists only of the identity element).
#Two free groups <math>F_S</math> and <math>F_T</math> are isomorphic if and only if <math>S</math> and <math>T</math> have the same [[cardinality]]. This cardinality is called the '''rank''' of the free group <math>F</math>. Thus for every [[cardinal number]] ''k'', there is, [[up to]] isomorphism, exactly one free group of rank ''k''.
#A free group of finite rank ''n'' > 1 has an [[exponential growth|exponential]] [[growth rate (group theory)|growth rate]] of order 2''n'' − 1.

A few other related results are:
#The [[Nielsen–Schreier theorem]]:  Every [[subgroup]] of a free group is free. Furthermore, if the free group <math>F</math> has rank ''n'' and the subgroup <math>H</math> has [[Index of a subgroup|index]] ''e'' in <math>F</math>, then <math>H</math> is free of rank 1 + ''e''(''n–''1).
#A free group of rank ''k'' clearly has subgroups of every rank less than ''k''. Less obviously, a (''nonabelian!'') free group of rank at least 2 has subgroups of all [[countable set|countable]] ranks.
#The [[commutator subgroup]] of a free group of rank ''k'' > 1 has infinite rank; for example for <math>F(a,b)</math>, it is freely generated by the [[commutator]]s <math>[a^m,b^n]</math> for non-zero ''m'' and ''n''.
#The free group in two elements is [[SQ universal]]; the above follows as any SQ universal group has subgroups of all countable ranks.
#Any group that [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] on a tree, [[free action|freely]] and preserving the [[oriented graph|orientation]], is a free group of countable rank (given by 1 plus the [[Euler characteristic]] of the [[Group action (mathematics)|quotient]] [[graph theory|graph]]).
#The [[Cayley graph]] of a free group of finite rank, with respect to a free generating set, is a [[tree (graph theory)|tree]] on which the group acts freely, preserving the orientation. As a topological space (a one-dimensional [[simplicial complex]]), this Cayley graph <math>\Gamma(F)</math> is [[Contractible space|contractible]]. For a finitely presented group <math>G</math>, the natural homomorphism defined above, <math>\varphi:F\to G</math>, defines a [[Covering space|covering map]] of Cayley graphs <math>\varphi^*:\Gamma(F)\to\Gamma(G)</math>, in fact a universal covering. Hence, the [[fundamental group]] of the Cayley graph <math>\Gamma(G)</math> is isomorphic to the kernel of <math>\varphi</math>, the normal subgroup of relations among the generators of <math>G</math>. The extreme case is when <math>G=\{e\}</math>, the trivial group, considered with as many generators as <math>F</math>, all of them trivial; the Cayley graph <math>\Gamma(G)</math> is a bouquet of circles, and its fundamental group is <math>F</math> itself.
#Any subgroup of a free group, <math>H \subset F</math>, corresponds to a covering space of the bouquet of circles, namely to the [[Schreier coset graph]] of <math>F/H</math>. This can be used to give a topological proof of the Nielsen-Schreier theorem above.
#The [[groupoid]] approach to these results, given in the work by P.J. Higgins below, is related to the use of [[covering space]]s above. It allows more powerful results, for example on [[Grushko's theorem]], and a normal form for the fundamental groupoid of a graph of groups. In this approach there is considerable use of free groupoids on a directed graph.
# [[Grushko's theorem]] has the consequence that if a subset <math>B</math> of a free group <math>F</math> on  ''n'' elements generates <math>F</math> and has ''n'' elements, then <math>B</math> generates <math>F</math> freely.

== Free abelian group ==
{{further|Free abelian group}}

The free abelian group on a set <math>S</math> is defined via its universal property in the analogous way, with obvious modifications:
Consider a pair <math>(F,\varphi)</math>, where <math>F</math> is an abelian group and <math>\varphi:S\to F</math> is a function. <math>F</math> is said to be the '''free abelian group on <math>S</math> with respect to <math>\varphi</math> ''' if for any abelian group <math>G</math> and any function <math>\psi:S\to G</math>, there exists a unique homomorphism <math>f:F\to G</math> such that
<math display="block">f(\varphi(s))=\psi(s),\ \forall s\in S.</math>

The free abelian group on <math>S</math> can be explicitly identified as the free group <math>F(S)</math> modulo the subgroup generated by its commutators, <math>[F(S),F(S)]</math>, i.e.
its [[abelianisation]]. In other words, the free abelian group on <math>S</math> is the set of words that are distinguished only up to the order of letters. The rank of a free group can therefore also be defined as the rank of its abelianisation as a free abelian group.

==Tarski's problems==
Around 1945, [[Alfred Tarski]] asked whether the free groups on two or more generators have the same [[model theory|first-order theory]], and whether this theory is [[decidability (logic)|decidable]]. {{harvtxt|Sela|2006}} answered the first question by showing that any two nonabelian free groups have the same first-order theory, and {{harvtxt|Kharlampovich|Myasnikov|2006}} answered both questions, showing that this theory is decidable.

A similar unsolved (as of 2011) question in [[free probability theory]] asks whether the [[von Neumann group algebra]]s of any two non-abelian finitely generated free groups are isomorphic.
